threat_assessment:
WHAT TURNS THE TABLE. Two boards and one sentence.

Miirym plus any one of Dragon Tempest, Terror of the Peaks or Scourge of Valkas. Anyone who has seen this deck knows the next nontoken Dragon is copied and priced in damage.

Panharmonicon joining that board. One Lathliss cast out of it is 64 damage in twelve aimed instances, enough to kill a seat at 40 (stacks 002 and 007).

Then the sentence. In log 003 the table converged inside one cycle of hearing "Sean is swinging for 28 in the air". Do the arithmetic in your head and say the number only on the turn it is lethal.

WHAT V6 CHANGES. You used to tap out to build that board. Four of the six additions work on somebody else's turn — Stubborn Denial is an instant; Mithril Coat, Transcendent Dragon and Whirlwing Stormbrood have flash — so the board can arrive at the end of the turn before yours rather than in front of a table with a full cycle to price it. Whirlwing is what converts the rest: while it is on the battlefield your sorceries and your Dragon spells have flash too. Put the payoff down on a quiet turn; put the Dragon down at an end step.

Two of the six are measured at a table. In the 177-game standard-v3 Forge run behind these swaps, Mithril Coat was cast 40 times and activated 35, and Steel Hellkite cast 36 and activated 53. Whirlwing Stormbrood is not measured at all: Forge cannot load it and logged "an unsupported card was requested" fourteen times, so the flash grant this plan rests on has never been simulated.

SIGNALS, AND THE ASSUMPTION UNDER EACH. Four untapped sources with two blue among them, held through your whole turn: that seat is holding a counter more often than not. It is a read, not a fact — price it and cast your second-scariest piece into it. Mana up two turns running with nothing cast: a sweeper for your wave. Deploy across two turns and keep {1}{G}, {2}{W} or {3} available for Heroic Intervention, Teferi's Protection or Mithril Coat.

WHAT YOU WILL MISPRICE. Flawless Maneuver and Deflecting Swat each ask you to control a commander, and The Ur-Dragon is on the battlefield by turn six in 0.333 of runs. Budget {2}{W} and {2}{R}, not zero.

No game has been played on this 99. The only table data is 100 Forge games on the v1.0.0 list against a pod since retired — 12 wins across 86 decided games, 0.14, ci95 [0.082, 0.228], eliminated in 75 of 100, and 0.23 interaction spells cast a game against 0.42 received. That last pair is the deck V6 exists to replace.
matchups:
VS SWEEPER CONTROL. They hold the wrath for your wave and your wave is four permanents wide. Deploy across two turns and keep what rebuilds — Miirym and Lathliss rebuild in tokens. V6 means you no longer have to guess the turn: cast Whirlwing Stormbrood, then put the Dragons down at the end of their turn, after the sweeper was not cast. Heroic Intervention at {1}{G} and Teferi's Protection at {2}{W} cover the whole board. One of the protection-or-response group is in hand by turn six in 0.713 of runs. Exactly two cards answer a spell on the stack: Stubborn Denial and Transcendent Dragon. Denial is a hard counter only while you control a creature with power 4 or greater — 21 of the 32 creature cards in this deck qualify — so it is live from the first real Dragon and a {1} tax before that.

VS STAX AND TAX. You are the beatdown; race the lock. A tax lands where you are thinnest: 22 nonland entries sit at mana value five or more, the nine-mana commander among them, against 5.948 mean available mana on turn five. Point Generous Gift, Swords to Plowshares or Chaos Warp at the piece that taxes you, not at the biggest body.

VS GO-WIDE AND AGGRO. Your Dragons block for free. Crux of Fate's non-Dragon mode is asymmetric on purpose and the price is exactly eight cards: Birds of Paradise, Bloom Tender, Delighted Halfling, Faeburrow Elder, Ignoble Hierarch, Dragonlord's Servant, Dragonspeaker Shaman and Solphim, Mayhem Dominus. Count black before you plan around it — {3}{B}{B} on 21 sources is 0.729 on curve. Steel Hellkite is the cleaner answer and it is new: activate for X = 0 on a turn it dealt that player combat damage and every token and every Treasure they control is destroyed.

VS COMBO AND DRAIN. Present the board early and keep one response up. Stubborn Denial for {U} answers the noncreature half. Transcendent Dragon at {4}{U}{U} counters, exiles and lets you cast the spell yourself, and it is a body every payoff you control fires on. Then attack the assembling seat every turn from the moment you name it — in log 004 the seat nobody attacked won with a tap-untap engine while the table spent its removal on you. One hole is real and deck-audit prices it: four permanent classes answered against a floor of five, with graveyard uncovered. Reading every oracle text in the 99, the only card that mentions a graveyard at all is Transcendent Dragon, exiling what it counters. Spend removal on whatever fills a graveyard, never on what comes back out of one.
how_it_wins:
The deck charges the table for every Dragon that ARRIVES. The attack is a bonus you collect.

Eminence bills from the command zone on turn one: every other Dragon spell costs {1} less, with nothing on the battlefield to remove. Four printed reducers stack on top of it — Urza's Incubator, Dragonspeaker Shaman, Herald's Horn, Dragonlord's Servant. What that buys is not one cheap Dragon, it is two in one turn, and every trigger downstream is priced against that.

Then the payoffs charge for each arrival. Dragon Tempest, Terror of the Peaks and Scourge of Valkas pay only for what lands after them, so the order is payoff, then Miirym or Lathliss, then the Dragon.

That board is proven twice. With Miirym, Panharmonicon, Terror of the Peaks and Dragon Tempest down, one Lathliss cast is 64 damage in twelve separately aimed instances, and every instance reads any target — pointed at one seat the running total is 6, 12, 16, 20, 26, 32, 37, 42, so a player at 40 dies (stacks 002 and 007). Ancient Gold Dragon connecting is the larger shape: fifteen entries on one instruction, 255 available (stack 001).

The commander is the name of the deck, not the plan. Mean cast turn 6.881, median 7, on the battlefield by turn six in 0.333 of runs, never inside ten turns in 2,277 of 10,000. Hellkite Courser puts it there for {4}{R}{R} instead of nine.

What has to be true is mana. 35 land copies, land drops 0.756 on turn four and 0.615 on turn five, and two stalled turns in a row in 0.0793 of runs, ci95 [0.0742, 0.0848] — worse than any tracked deck, with 3,801 of the 4,321 stalled turns mana-short rather than empty-handed.

And the thing the table misreads: unopposed, this kills one seat by turn seven — median 7, 0.297 by turn six. A pod reads that speed off your board before you can use it, and five games at 1W 4L say it kills you first. V6 answers that with flash, not with more speed.

combo_lines.001:
The word that decides this is nontoken. Fifteen Faerie Dragons arrive on one instruction and not one of them qualifies, so Miirym copies nothing at all. Dragon Tempest carries no such reservation: one event with fifteen occurrences is fifteen separate triggers (CR 603.2c), each choosing its target as it goes on the stack (CR 115.1d) and each counting your Dragons again at its own resolution (CR 608.2h). Seventeen damage, fifteen times, with priority passing between every instalment.

What it proves: 255 available at a single target, and the 30-life seat dead on the second trigger aimed there. What it does not prove is that you arrive here. The board is granted a connected Ancient Gold Dragon and the d20 is fixed at 15. Arithmetic on the printed card puts the real threshold lower — with N tokens each trigger deals N+2 and there are N of them, so three seats at 40 needs twelve tokens, which is a roll of 12 or better — but that is arithmetic, not a checked line. Aim carefully: a trigger still pointed at a player who has already lost is removed on resolution (CR 608.2b).
combo_lines.002:
Panharmonicon does not read the trigger, only what caused it — an artifact or creature entering — so Miirym's "another nontoken Dragon" and Terror of the Peaks's "another creature" are treated alike, and each triggers again (CR 603.2d). The cascade is finite for one reason: the copies are tokens, and every nontoken clause in the chain steps over them.

What it proves: two nonlegendary Lathliss copies and 64 damage in twelve separately aimed instances — 36 from Terror, 28 from Tempest at X = 4, 4, 5, 5, 5, 5 — on the trigger ordering the resolution names. Order it any other way and you lose four.

And it proves one more thing. Every instance says any target, so all twelve may name the same player. Aimed at one seat the running total is 6, 12, 16, 20, 26, 32, 37, 42, and the seat is at 3 before the eighth instance, so nothing fizzles: this board kills a fresh 40-life player. The resolution's line about the 40-life opponent surviving at 8 is the assignment it chose, not a ceiling.

What it does not prove: two seats. 64 is less than 72.
combo_lines.005:
Two zones settle it. Sneak Attack reaches a creature card in your hand; a commander begins the game in the command zone (CR 903.6), and the command zone is not the hand. So the line that cheats The Ur-Dragon past its nine mana does not exist.

Everything below the command zone is affirmed. Drakuseth enters for {R}; its ability fires because it was declared as an attacker rather than cast (CR 508.3a); haste makes that attack legal (CR 702.10b); and the 17 damage already dealt is not undone by the mandatory end-step sacrifice (CR 610.1).

What it proves: {R} buys 17 damage, a dead 2/2 and one turn. What it does not: any route to your commander.

Hellkite Courser is the one card in the 99 whose text does reach that zone, and its line is still UNPROVEN. Stack 008 resolves it and the checker FAILED it — the four answers stand, two of the proofs under them did not, and a revision is in flight. Treat it as a reading: {4}{R}{R} puts the commander onto the battlefield and the haste goes to the COMMANDER rather than to the Courser.
combo_lines.007:
This is stack 002's board with Panharmonicon removed and nothing else changed, resolved because a cut list proposed cutting it.

Miirym triggers once, so one token copy enters instead of two: 20 damage in four instances — Terror 6 and 6, Tempest 4 and 4 — against 64 in twelve. That is not a halving. It is 68.75% gone, because the doubler was doubling Terror and both Dragon Tempest abilities on every entry as well as doubling Miirym, and losing Miirym's second trigger also deletes the second token and its whole wave of entry triggers.

What it proves: the 32-life seat survives at 12, and the margin cannot be closed on that board — the resolution checked the only activated ability available, the {1}{R} Dragon pump, and the declared mana does not stretch to it once Lathliss is paid for (CR 601.2f, CR 601.2h). Cutting Panharmonicon costs stack 002 its lethality, not its margin.

It also settles what 002 left open. Twelve instances that each read any target may all name one player, so 002's board kills a seat at 40. This one does not reach 40 at all.

card_roles.The Ur-Dragon: Your discount engine, and it bills from the command zone — every other Dragon spell costs {1} less whether or not he ever touches the battlefield. Cast him only when nine mana is genuinely spare; the attack trigger that draws per attacking Dragon and drops a free permanent is a bonus you collect, never a turn you plan.
card_roles.Ancient Gold Dragon: One connection rolls a d20 and hands you that many flying bodies, which is your single biggest swing with Dragon Tempest already down (stack 001). Point it at the emptiest board at the table, not the scariest one.
card_roles.Arcane Signet: Two-mana any-colour fixing in a five-colour deck. Play it on turn two ahead of almost anything else you could be doing.
card_roles.Blasphemous Act: It costs {1} less per creature on the battlefield, so by the time you want it the table has usually made it a one-mana reset. With Wrathful Red Dragon out it stops being a reset and becomes an execution (stack 004).
card_roles.Boros Charm: Four to the face, indestructible for everything you own, or double strike on one Dragon — pick the mode that ends the turn. The indestructible mode is your cheapest way through a sweeper, so hold it for that first.
card_roles.Breaching Dragonstorm: It digs to the first nonland card and casts it free at mana value 8 or less, which describes most of your top end. Fire it on a turn you need a body immediately, not on a turn you want value.
card_roles.Cavern-Hoard Dragon: It costs {X} less for the artifacts an opponent controls, so it lands early against Treasure and equipment seats and mints Treasures back on every hit. Its pairing with Aggravated Assault still needs a stack scenario — take the body and the mana, not the promise.
card_roles.Chaos Warp: Your only clean answer to a resolved artifact or enchantment, and it hits any permanent at all. Aim it at whatever stops your combats, and accept that they reveal the top of their library and may keep a permanent off it.
card_roles.Chromatic Lantern: It turns every land you control into an any-colour source, which is worth far more than the one mana it makes itself. Play it the turn before you need a double-pip spell, never on the turn you already need it.
card_roles.Counterspell: Two mana to say no. Hold it for somebody's win attempt, not for the first scary creature you happen to see.
card_roles.Crux of Fate: Choose destroy all non-Dragon creatures and it is a one-sided wipe that leaves your board standing. The cost is Dragonspeaker Shaman and Rivaz of the Claw, who are the two creatures here that are not Dragons — count them before you cast it.
card_roles.Dovin's Veto: It counters the noncreature spell and cannot be countered itself. Save it for the combo piece or the sweeper, the two things that actually beat you.
card_roles.Dracogenesis: Every Dragon spell you cast is free while this is on the battlefield. Land it and empty your hand the same turn, because nobody is going to let you untap with it.
card_roles.Dragon Tempest: Two mana, and every Dragon entering afterwards throws damage equal to your Dragon count. Get it down before the Dragons — it pays nothing at all for what has already landed.
card_roles.Dragon's Hoard: Any-colour fixing that grows a gold counter per Dragon entering, and each counter cashes for a card. Play it early enough that the counters have time to stack up; it is real card advantage the role taxonomy does not credit.
card_roles.Dragonback Assault: Three damage on entry clears a small board, and afterwards every land drop is a 4/4 flier. It is your best single answer to a token pod — and it kills Dragonspeaker Shaman and Rivaz of the Claw, so sequence around them.
card_roles.Dragonlord Dromoka: Cannot be countered and shuts your opponents out of your turn entirely — this is the body you cast into open blue mana. It also makes your alpha strike safe from instant-speed tricks.
card_roles.Dragonlord Kolaghan: Haste for the whole team, which turns every fresh Dragon into damage the turn it lands. Treat the 10-life punisher clause as a coincidence you occasionally profit from, never a plan.
card_roles.Dragonspeaker Shaman: {2} off every Dragon spell for three mana, and the best turn-three play in the deck. Keep opening hands that contain it — a reducer only shows up by turn six 33.2% of the time.
card_roles.Drakuseth, Maw of Flames: Ten damage split across three targets every single time it attacks, before blockers matter at all. Cheat it in with Sneak Attack on the turn you need that damage right now (stack 005).
card_roles.Eerie Interlude: Blink your team out of a sweeper and they come back at end of turn, re-firing every enters trigger on the way in. Hold it as protection first and value second.
card_roles.Encroaching Dragonstorm: Two basics on arrival, and it bounces itself when a Dragon enters, so it is ramp you get to replay. Cast it on four when nothing better exists and re-buy it forever.
card_roles.Enlightened Tutor: One mana finds Aggravated Assault, Panharmonicon or whichever protection artifact you are missing. Cast it the turn before you need the card, never on the turn you do — it goes on top of your library, not into your hand.
card_roles.Farseek: It fetches any nonbasic with a basic land type, which covers the shocks and the Triomes in this list. Two mana that ramps and fixes at once, and you should almost always take the dual.
card_roles.Flawless Maneuver: Free while you control a commander, and your whole team becomes indestructible. Never let it rot in hand while you decline to commit the board — and price it at three mana in the games where the commander never lands.
card_roles.Garruk's Uprising: Trample for the team and a card every time a 4-power creature enters, which is nearly every creature you play. This is the draw engine the audit says you are six cards short of.
card_roles.Generous Gift: Three mana destroys any permanent and hands back a 3/3. Spend it on the thing that beats you, not on the biggest body at the table.
card_roles.Goldspan Dragon: A hasty 5-power flier that mints a Treasure whenever it attacks or gets targeted, and its Treasures make two mana each. That is unrestricted mana, so it is one of the few things here that can legally pay Aggravated Assault.
card_roles.Hellkite Courser: This is the card that genuinely pulls The Ur-Dragon out of the command zone — hasty, for one attack, with the eminence draw trigger live and no tax added (stack 005). Attack with everything the turn it enters.
card_roles.Herald's Horn: {1} off every Dragon creature spell plus a free look at the top of your library each upkeep. Name Dragon and never think about it again.
card_roles.Heroic Intervention: Two mana buys hexproof and indestructible for every permanent you own. Hold it for the turn you commit the wave, which is the turn it is worth a card.
card_roles.Klauth, Unrivaled Ancient: Attacking adds mana equal to your attackers' total power, which is an enormous number and strictly for casting spells. Spend it on a second Dragon postcombat; it can never pay an activated ability, so it cannot fund Aggravated Assault.
card_roles.Lathliss, Dragon Queen: Every nontoken Dragon after her drags a 5/5 along, and her {1}{R} pump turns a stalled board into lethal. With Miirym, Panharmonicon, Terror of the Peaks and Dragon Tempest down, one cast of her is 64 damage (stack 002).
card_roles.Miirym, Sentinel Wyrm: She copies every nontoken Dragon you land after her, from behind ward {2}. Sequence her ahead of your top end and expect the table to answer her first — she is the scariest fair card you own.
card_roles.Mox Jasper: Free any-colour mana the moment you control a Dragon. Keep a Dragon on the battlefield and this is a land you never had to draw.
card_roles.Nature's Lore: Two mana for any Forest card, and it arrives untapped — your Forest-typed duals included. Take the dual over the basic unless you genuinely need green tomorrow.
card_roles.Old Gnawbone: Every point of combat damage your team deals comes back as Treasure, and Treasure is the one mana here that can pay Aggravated Assault. With Assault down, one unblocked connection ends the whole table in sequence (stack 006).
card_roles.Panharmonicon: It doubles every trigger caused by a creature entering — Miirym, Lathliss, Terror, Tempest, all of it (stack 002). Play it before the wave, never after it.
card_roles.Patriarch's Bidding: Name Dragon and everything you have lost comes back at once, including whatever a sweeper just ate. Save it for after the wrath, and remember every other player names something too.
card_roles.Relic of Legends: Any-colour mana, and it taps your untapped legendary creatures for more of it. In a list carrying 14 legendary permanents that is a Signet that grows all game.
card_roles.Return of the Wildspeaker: Draw cards equal to your biggest non-Human's power — usually five or seven here — or pump the team for the kill. It is an instant, so cast it after blockers are declared and let them choose wrong.
card_roles.Rishkar's Expertise: A giant refill off your largest body plus a free spell at mana value 5 or less. Cast it with Terror of the Peaks or Scourge of Valkas still in hand and take both halves.
card_roles.Rivaz of the Claw: Two mana in any colours toward Dragon creature spells, plus one Dragon recast from your graveyard each turn. Note what he is not: a 3/3 Lizard Warlock, so your own Dragonback Assault and Crux of Fate's non-Dragon mode both kill him, and his mana is spells-only and will never pay Aggravated Assault.
card_roles.Roiling Dragonstorm: Two mana to draw two and discard one, and it returns to your hand whenever a Dragon enters. Replay it every turn you have two mana lying idle.
card_roles.Sarkhan's Triumph: Instant-speed tutor for any Dragon in the deck — engine piece or answer body, your choice. Cast it at the end of the turn before your big one.
card_roles.Savage Ventmaw: Attacking adds {R}{R}{R}{G}{G}{G} that survives the phase change, which is a whole extra Dragon in your postcombat main. With Aggravated Assault it pays for its own extra combat and leaves {R} behind (stack 003).
card_roles.Scourge of Valkas: Damage equal to your Dragon count every time a Dragon enters, itself included. It is Dragon Tempest on a 4/4 flier, so land it before the flood rather than during it.
card_roles.Scourge of the Throne: Attack the player at the highest life and you untap all attackers for a free extra combat, once each turn. It is the only extra-combat effect in the 99 besides Aggravated Assault, so point the first attack at the table leader deliberately.
card_roles.Skyshroud Claim: Two Forest cards onto the battlefield untapped on turn four, and your Forest-typed duals qualify. It fixes while it ramps, which is the only thing turn four is for here.
card_roles.Sol Ring: Two colourless on turn one or two. Always keep it, always resolve it first.
card_roles.Swan Song: One mana answers the sweeper, the ritual or the enchantment; they get a 2/2 flier and you keep your board. Take that trade every time it is offered.
card_roles.Swords to Plowshares: One mana exiles anything, which is the cleanest answer in the 99. Spend it on the creature that beats you, not on the first one you meet.
card_roles.Teferi's Protection: Your board phases out and your life cannot change until your next turn. Hold it for the sweeper or the lethal swing — it is the best card you can have in hand on your big turn.
card_roles.Temur Ascendancy: Haste for everything and a card whenever a 4-power creature enters, which here means nearly every Dragon. Every body you cast attacks the same turn it lands.
card_roles.Terror of the Peaks: Every creature entering afterwards throws its own power at any target, and opponents pay three life just to aim a spell at it. Land it first, then flood the board.
card_roles.Thrakkus the Butcher: Attacking doubles the power of every Dragon you control, which is the fastest route from a fair board to a lethal one. Count the damage before you declare attackers; it usually kills somebody you did not expect.
card_roles.Tiamat: Casting it fetches five differently named Dragons straight to hand — take the engine pieces, not the biggest bodies. Eminence and the reducers make the seven-drop honest, and it is the one God card The World Tree can find.
card_roles.Urza's Incubator: {2} off every Dragon creature spell for three mana. Alongside Dragonspeaker Shaman it turns your entire top end into midrange.
card_roles.Utvara Hellkite: Every attacking Dragon brings a 6/6 flier with it, so one combat under this ends most boards. Keep it alive through a single turn cycle and the long game is already yours.
card_roles.Worldly Tutor: One mana at instant speed for any creature in the deck. Fetch the piece the turn before you need it, not the turn you are already dead.
card_roles.Aggravated Assault: The win condition and the loudest tell in one card: {3}{R}{R} untaps your team and buys another combat, and all three infinites in the 99 run through it. Hold it for the turn it kills somebody, and remember your Dragon-restricted mana cannot pay the activation.
card_roles.Korlessa, Scale Singer: Two mana lets you cast Dragons straight off the top of your library, with the top card always visible. She is a 1/4 Dragon, so your own Dragonback Assault does not touch her and Crux of Fate's non-Dragon mode leaves her standing — deploy her early and leave her there.
card_roles.Deflecting Swat: Free while you control a commander, and it re-aims any spell or ability — the removal pointed at Aggravated Assault, or somebody else's tutor. Keep a red source up on the turns that matter, because the commander is usually not on the battlefield to make it free.
card_roles.Wrathful Red Dragon: Damage dealt to your Dragons gets thrown at any non-Dragon target, so a sweeper becomes an execution: three Dragons dealt 13 is 39 at one opponent (stack 004). Get it down early and let them cast the wrath.
card_roles.Sneak Attack: One red mana puts any Dragon from your hand onto the battlefield with haste, and every attack and enters trigger fires before the end-step sacrifice (stack 005). It reaches your hand only — never plan on it for the commander.
card_roles.Atsushi, the Blazing Sky: A four-mana flier that pays you when it dies: two cards to play, or three Treasures that pay for anything, including Aggravated Assault. Block with it happily.
card_roles.Blood Crypt: Pay the 2 life and take it untapped. Black is your scarcest colour on curve at 26.1%, so the tempo beats the life almost every time.
card_roles.Breeding Pool: Your untapped green-blue source for Korlessa on turn two or Miirym on curve. The 2 life is cheap on the turns those matter.
card_roles.Canopy Vista: Green and white, untapped once two basics are down. Lead with basics early and this stops costing you a turn.
card_roles.Cinder Glade: Red and green untapped once you control two basics — the two colours this deck leans on hardest. Sequence a basic first and it is a dual.
card_roles.City of Brass: Any colour, untapped, for one damage a tap. In a five-colour deck that is the cheapest fixing you will ever buy; pay it and stop thinking about it.
card_roles.Clifftop Retreat: Red and white untapped as long as a Mountain or Plains is already down. Sequence your basics so that it is.
card_roles.Command Tower: Any of your five colours, untapped, for nothing at all. Play it the moment you draw it.
card_roles.Exotic Orchard: It reads your opponents' lands, so it is a second Command Tower at a multicolour table and much less at a mono-colour one. Check the board before you build a turn on it.
card_roles.Fabled Passage: Fetch a basic, and it untaps once four lands are down. Go get the colour you are actually missing — usually the Swamp or the Island — not the one you already have three of.
card_roles.Forbidden Orchard: Any colour untapped, and each tap hands an opponent a 1/1. Tap it when the mana matters more than the chump blocker you are donating.
card_roles.Forest: Green for Nature's Lore, Farseek and the green half of Savage Ventmaw. Green is your most reliable colour at 84.9% on curve precisely because of these.
card_roles.Glacial Fortress: White and blue untapped if a Plains or Island is already down — your two thinnest colours, so drop it on a turn you can afford to have it tapped.
card_roles.Haven of the Spirit Dragon: Colourless, or any colour that may only cast a Dragon creature spell, plus a late buy-back for a dead Dragon. Never count its coloured mana toward an activated ability.
card_roles.Island: Your only blue basic, and therefore the Counterspell and Korlessa source. Fetch it with Fabled Passage when you are holding either.
card_roles.Jetmir's Garden: Three colours on a tapped land, or a {3} cycle when you are flooded out. Play it on a turn you were never going to spend everything anyway.
card_roles.Maelstrom of the Spirit Dragon: Colourless, or Dragon-spell-only colour, and it sacrifices itself later to find a Dragon. Like Haven, its coloured mana casts and never activates.
card_roles.Mountain: Your most-demanded colour on a land that always comes in untapped — red is 46.5% of your pips. Fetch these first when a triple-red spell is in hand.
card_roles.Overgrown Tomb: Black and green untapped for 2 life. Black sources are scarce enough here that you should almost always pay it.
card_roles.Path of Ancestry: It enters tapped, but every creature it casts that shares a type with your commander scries, and nearly every creature you play does. Drop it on a turn you were not spending all your mana.
card_roles.Reflecting Pool: It copies whatever your other lands can make, so it is superb late and close to blank on turn one. Hold it behind a real dual whenever you can.
card_roles.Rootbound Crag: Red and green untapped once a Mountain or Forest is down. Sequence basics first and it never costs you tempo.
card_roles.Savage Lands: Three colours, always tapped — one of only five lands here that give you no choice about it. Play it on a turn where a tapped land costs you nothing.
card_roles.Steam Vents: Blue and red for 2 life. Take it untapped whenever you want Counterspell live inside this turn cycle.
card_roles.Stomping Ground: Red and green for 2 life — the two colours your curve leans on hardest, so pay it more often than you don't.
card_roles.Sulfur Falls: Blue and red untapped once an Island or Mountain is down. It is your smoothest way to hold up a counter and still cast a Dragon.
card_roles.Swamp: Your single black basic, and the fetch target that turns on Patriarch's Bidding or Crux of Fate. Go get it the moment either is in hand.
card_roles.The World Tree: Green while it stands alone, and all-colour fixing for every land you control once six are down. Its ten-mana ability puts Tiamat onto the battlefield — she is the only God card in the 99, so it finds exactly one thing.
card_roles.Unclaimed Territory: Name Dragon and it makes any colour for your creature spells. That mana casts; it never activates.
card_roles.Ziatora's Proving Ground: Black, red and green on a tapped land, or a {3} cycle when your lands are already plentiful. Take the fixing early and the cycle late.

mulligan:
Mulligan on colours and on your cheapest spell, not on land count. You can afford to ship: the simulator keeps 0.773 of first sevens at 0.279 mean mulligans.

The keep that decides games is three lands, a mana creature and a cost reducer. Urza's Incubator, Dragonspeaker Shaman, Herald's Horn, Dragonlord's Servant — one of those in an opener and you stop reading the hand. A reducer arrives by turn six in only 0.421 of runs, reducer plus ramp in 0.337.

Also keep: two lands with Sol Ring, Arcane Signet or Talisman of Dominance; three lands with Farseek, Nature's Lore or Skyshroud Claim and a Dragon at mana value five or less.

Ship a hand with no green source — the pilot's own rule after log 005, where Farseek and the green Dragons sat in hand all game. Ship a hand whose cheapest spell costs five; that was log 002's keep and the mana never arrived. Ship three lands, one rock and two Dragons at five or more with no reducer; that was log 006's keep, which the pilot does not stand by.

What those rules are really about is the stall. Land drops fall to 0.756 on turn four and 0.615 on turn five, so the bridge does not arrive later.

Do not keep for black. One card in the 99 wants it — Crux of Fate at {3}{B}{B} — on 21 sources against a yardstick of 30, 0.729 on curve.

V6 changes one line. Protection or a response is in hand by turn six in 0.713 of runs, and the cheapest of them, Stubborn Denial, costs {U}. A hand with a blue source, a threat and one spare mana is now a hand that can act on somebody else's turn. It is still a bonus and not a keep: you can cast an answer on turn six in 0.510 of runs against 0.890 holding one, and the model calls that figure a floor.
upgrades:
Six of these ten buy mana or buy a discount. Nobody picked that theme — it is 34 land copies against a 36-38 band, doing arithmetic out loud. Land drops hit 60.3% on turn five and 49.7% on turn six, mean available mana at turn six is 4.937, and opposite that number sit 28 of 66 nonland entries at mana value five or more.

The four mana picks are four shapes of one complaint. Ancient Tomb is two mana out of one land — and deck-facts flags five lands here whose mana cannot pay an activated ability at all, where the Tomb's can. Mana Confluence is five colours untapped where red sits at 27 sources against a 36 target while carrying 47 of the deck's 101 pips. Bojuka Bog is a 35th land copy that happens to do a second job.

Three Visits is pure timing. The obsolescence index rates it against Skyshroud Claim at 0.9936 similarity on a lower mana value — the same effect on turn two, where the curve is intact, rather than turn four, where it is bending.

The discount pair is the biggest percentage swing on the page. The declared reducer group is three cards: 19.9% of openers, 42.3% measured, 33.2% of them by turn six. Ruby Medallion and Sarkhan, Soul Aflame take it to five, which the corpus prices at 31% of openers — and the Medallion's discount reaches 32 of this deck's cards, red being where nearly half the pips live.

Then the ceiling. The extra-combat ignition assembles 6.4% of the time overall and 3.6% by turn six, at a mean turn of 5.442 — one game in sixteen. Hellkite Charger at six mana and Najeela, the Blade-Blossom at three are second and third routes to it, and Gamble is a one-mana line to the enchantment itself. The two combo lines those creatures open have no stack artifact behind them yet; the record on them is open.

Soul-Guide Lantern is the cheap outlier and the only pick that moves an axis by itself: one mana, graveyard answers from 0 to 1, interaction classes from 4 to 5. And the slate is bracket-neutral — all ten leave the computed floor at 4.
mana_base:
Thirty-four land copies across 29 entries, against the 36 to 38 the template asks for. Sixteen print 'enters tapped' somewhere — 47%, which reads as a disaster — but only five enter tapped unconditionally, against a ceiling of eight. The tapland axis passes comfortably. The land count is what misses.

The bill lands on tempo: 3.042 mana on turn three, 4.937 on turn six, 6.539 on turn ten, the land drop holding at 88.3% on turn three and then falling through 60.3% and 49.7% — exactly the turns a deck with 28 five-plus-drops has to deploy. This base rarely misses a colour. It misses turns.

Pip share and source share disagree hardest on red: 46.5% of the pip load on 28.6% of the sources, 47 pips across 32 cards, as many as three in one cost. Green is nearly square at 21.8% of pips on 25.7% of sources, and its lands keep pace — 84.9% on curve from lands alone against red's 58.0%, because green asks one pip at a time where red's effective ask is two. Black runs it backwards, 7.9% of pips on 15.7% of sources, and still finishes worst at 26.1%: a six-card splash on 11 land sources.

Six rocks and three dorks close the gaps unevenly — black to 44.6%, red to 76.4%, white to 78.7%, blue to 81.0%, green to 92.7%. Five of the nine make any colour: Arcane Signet, Chromatic Lantern, Dragon's Hoard, Mox Jasper, Relic of Legends. That is why sources pass at 46 against a floor of 45 while the land count fails. The fixing does the colour work; the lands only do the mana.

The 90% yardstick wants 36 black and 36 red sources inside a 34-land deck — a measuring stick, not a possibility, and it reads that way in every five-colour list. It refuses two things: the five sources making spells-only mana, real for casting and worth nothing to an activated ability, and Treasures out of Old Gnawbone, Goldspan Dragon, Atsushi and Cavern-Hoard Dragon, income nobody forecasts from your lands.
editors_letter:
The card on the front of this deck costs nine mana, and the argument in the Pilot's Log is about whether you should ever pay it.

The Ur-Dragon has an ability that runs from the command zone, the one place nobody can reach. Whether that ability is what actually carries the deck is what the panel fights over, and it is a better fight than I expected.

What the deck does meanwhile is put enormous fliers onto the table in waves and charge everybody for each one. One Dragon arriving becomes three. Each arrival is priced in damage, or cards, or Treasure. Underneath it sits one enchantment your whole table can name on sight, which is either how you win or why you get attacked first — a distinction Counselor Dictum spends most of the log drawing.

Coach Brightside opens by telling you to stop trying to cast your commander. He is right, his reasoning has not been proved, and he loses a second argument later about how fast the famous loop kills. Ledger has the rate that settles the first; the Counselor has the arithmetic that settles the second. Watch him take both.

You will have a good time here if you like being enormous and patient at once — a battlecruiser with a certified escape hatch it mostly does not need. You will not, if you want your win legible on turn four. This deck asks you to hold five colours and a top-heavy hand and trust that everyone else's clock is slower than yours.

pilots_log.text: Stop trying to cast your commander. I mean it as a keep decision: take the nine-mana Dragon out of the maths entirely, because the card this whole deck is named after is the one card in it you will almost never put on the battlefield, and the deck was built by somebody who already knew that. Ledger has the rate and it is worse than you are guessing. And before you take the reason from me — Counselor, what have any of us actually proved about why that is fine? I have a feeling your answer costs me something.

It costs you, and it costs you in the direction you did not pick.

Start with what is on the record, because there is less of it than the Coach's delivery suggests. Nothing in this deck's file resolves eminence. The Ur-Dragon reads "other Dragon spells you cast cost {1} less to cast", and I can read that to you all afternoon, but not one checker-passed stack has run a Dragon spell through the discount and measured what came out. That is why the file draws that arrow dashed. The Coach's conclusion is sound and his reason is unearned, and those are different things.

Note also the word "other". Whatever the discount is worth, it is worth nothing toward the nine. The commander does not make himself cheaper, and whether the deck's three reducers do — and whether they stack — is listed in this deck's open questions, unanswered.

What the record does hold about this commander is a refutation. Stack 005: he began the game in the command zone (CR 903.6), the hand is where a player holds cards that have been drawn (CR 402.1), and Sneak Attack reaches only "a creature card from your hand". Two zones, and no bridge between them. Sneak Attack cannot cheat your commander in. One card in the 99 can, because it names the zone out loud — Hellkite Courser, "you may put a commander you own from the command zone onto the battlefield", hasted, and returned there at the beginning of the next end step, with no cast added to the tax. That last is me reading printed text rather than holding up a ruling, and I will say so every time.

The holding: he is right that you will not be casting the commander. He has not yet earned the reason he gave you.

Ten thousand seeded runs. Commander cast at a mean turn of 8.967, median turn 9, 0% by turn six. In 8,634 of the ten thousand he is not cast inside ten turns at all. Of the runs that do get there, 618 land on turn nine and 449 on turn ten.

Mean available mana: 4.937 at turn six, 5.787 at turn eight, 6.539 at turn ten. The cost is nine.

A correction to my own figures before either of them spends them. The simulation does not model cost reduction. Every number above is a floor, and the size of what it leaves out is the quantity the Counselor has just told you nobody has measured.

Fewer than one game in seven, and that is the generous end. Taken — both of you, and it makes my advice better rather than worse.

So here is the hand you are keeping. Lands that make more than one colour. Something on two that makes mana. A Dragon you can actually pay for around five. If the nine-drop is sitting in that hand it is a spare card and you keep the hand anyway, because he was never in the hand's job description. He is doing whatever he is doing from a zone nobody at the table can point removal at.

The hand he just described has a name in the declaration and a number under it. Reducer plus ramp — the turn-five commander hand — assembles in 33.9% of runs, 23.1% by turn six, mean turn 4.645.

Its two halves are not the same size. Ramp or fixing is nine cards: 49.8% of opening sevens, 81.7% assembled, 71.6% by turn six, mean turn 2.588. The reducers are three cards — Urza's Incubator, Herald's Horn, Dragonspeaker Shaman — at 19.9% of opening sevens, 42.3% assembled, 33.2% by turn six. That is the thinnest declared thing in this deck that is not the combo.

What the fixing is up against: 28 of 66 nonland entries at mana value five or more, 34 land copies, and land drops at 88.3% on turn three, 73.9% on four, 60.3% on five, 49.7% on six. Sources held against a 90% target: red 27 of 36, green 24 of 22, blue 16 of 22, white 15 of 22.

Now the other card, the one you already know I mean. Aggravated Assault.

Three mana to put down, five to push the button, untap everything and take another combat, and with the right Dragon on the board it does not stop. My whole rule for it is one sentence: it is the last permanent you deploy, not the first. Not because it is precious. Because you own exactly one, the whole table can read it from across the room, and the moment it hits they stop caring about anybody else. Sit on it. Play the boring Dragon instead. Then one turn you untap, put it down, push the button, and it is over in a couple of swings.

Two swings. Let us establish which two, because the pairing is on the record twice and the two records do not say the same thing.

Stack 006 is Old Gnawbone and Aggravated Assault alone, with five untapped lands. The 7/7 connects, seven Treasures enter, the activation takes five of them, net two a cycle, and the lands are never touched all night. Opponent one at 40 is dead on combat six. Opponent two at 38, holding a ground 2/2 that cannot block a flier, is dead on combat twelve. Twenty-two Treasures on the table when the game ends. That is unbounded, and unbounded is not a synonym for fast.

Stack 003 is Savage Ventmaw and the same enchantment, and it is where the Coach's two swings came from — wrongly, and it is the easiest misreading in this deck to make. That stack has Old Gnawbone attacking as well. Its eleven damage a combat is Gnawbone's seven plus Ventmaw's four. What step 6 establishes for the named pair is the mana and nothing else: the attack trigger adds {R}{R}{R}{G}{G}{G}, Ventmaw's own text keeps it through the phase change, the {3} is paid with green because generic mana accepts any type (CR 107.4b), and one red is left floating. One attack funds one reactivation with change.

Savage Ventmaw alone puts four into a forty-life seat. Four into forty is the tenth combat, and that last step is arithmetic rather than a ruling, so I say so.

The tenth combat. All right — that one lands, and it changes something I have been saying at tables.

You are not looking for the loop. You are looking for the loop with the seven-power Dragon in it. Old Gnawbone takes a seat out six combats in and funds itself twice over on the way. Savage Ventmaw with nobody else swinging is you doing the same thing ten times in a row while three players get ten turns to find an answer. Same enchantment, completely different evening.

So when the small one is what you have, do not sit there grinding it solo. Take the extra combats and send the rest of your board with it. That is what an extra combat is actually for.

The two plans, priced side by side.

The loop: Aggravated Assault is a declared component of one card, 7.1% of an opening seven. Joined to a mana Dragon it assembles in 6.4% of runs, 3.6% by turn six, mean turn 5.442.

The Dragon payoff — Dragon Tempest, Terror of the Peaks, Scourge of Valkas, Lathliss, Miirym, Temur Ascendancy, Garruk's Uprising — is seven cards: 41.2% of opening sevens, 73.1% assembled, 62.2% by turn six, mean turn 2.865.

Seventeen times the assembly rate by turn six. The loop is the ceiling. It is not the plan.

And the component the loop leans on is three cards only if you do not read the third one.

The declared fuel half is Old Gnawbone, Savage Ventmaw and Cavern-Hoard Dragon. Cavern-Hoard reads "you create a Treasure token for each artifact that player controls", and "that player" is the player it just hit. Not you. Against a seat holding no artifacts it makes nothing, and it needs that seat holding five to cover one activation. It appears in neither of the loop's passing stacks. The combo database certifies it as a two-card infinite and the bracket report counts it; a database record is a claim somebody else made, and this magazine's word for proof is a stack that passed a checker.

Two more for the pilot's card. Five of your own mana sources cannot pay for the button: Klauth and Rivaz are spell-locked outright, and Haven of the Spirit Dragon, Maelstrom of the Spirit Dragon and Unclaimed Territory each carry a colourless mode that pays the {3} and can never touch the {R}{R}. Klauth can attack, make a fortune, and spend none of it here. And the hedge everybody reaches for, Scourge of the Throne, is in none of the six passing stacks — whether its extra combat re-fires the per-attacking-Dragon triggers is an open question in this file and I will not pretend otherwise. Enlightened Tutor is the only card in the 99 that can go and find the enchantment.

Which is exactly why I want you to stop treating this as a combo deck that sometimes attacks.

It is an attacking deck that sometimes combos. Your median game is you putting a Dragon down, the table taking damage for the privilege of you having done it, and then doing that again. Miirym turns one arrival into two. Panharmonicon turns Miirym into twice Miirym. Dragon Tempest charges everybody for every single arrival, and the price goes up each time because it is counting your board.

That is the game. Build the board. Make arriving expensive for them.

And unlike the discount, that part is on the record three times over.

Stack 002 is the cascade. Miirym, Panharmonicon, Dragon Tempest and Terror of the Peaks already down, and you cast one Lathliss. Panharmonicon doubles every trigger in the chain because each one is caused by a creature entering, so Miirym makes two nonlegendary 6/6 hasty copies, and the arrivals pay Terror 36 and Tempest 28 — sixty-four damage across twelve separately targeted instances. The 32-life seat dies. The 40 survives at 8.

Stack 001 is the burst. Ancient Gold Dragon connects, fifteen Faerie Dragons enter as one event, Dragon Tempest triggers fifteen times, and every trigger sees X equal to seventeen. The 30-life seat is dead to the second trigger aimed at it.

Stack 004 is the inversion. Blasphemous Act destroys all nine creatures on the table including all three of your own Dragons, and Wrathful Red Dragon still yields exactly three redirect triggers of 13 by last known information. Thirty-nine damage kills a 32-life seat, or drops a 40 to 1. Never both, and I have heard that sentence misquoted.

The brake is printed on the pieces, which is the elegant part. Every later arrival in the cascade is a token, and both "nontoken" clauses exclude tokens. The clause that makes the engine large is the clause that stops it being infinite.

One set of figures to sit against all of that.

Mean creatures on your battlefield: 0.628 at turn four, 1.010 at turn five, 1.463 at turn six, 2.456 at turn eight, 3.476 at turn ten. The Counselor's cascade has four permanents down before the Lathliss is cast. Her burst board counts seventeen Dragons.

Protection held for the big turn: eight cards, 45.6% of opening sevens, 77.1% assembled, 66.0% by turn six, mean turn 2.778. Payoff joined to a castable Dragon: 40.1% assembled, 26.8% by turn six, mean turn 4.721. Opening sevens kept without a mulligan: 75.1%, mean mulligans 0.313.

The simulation runs ten turns and models no interaction, no removal and no cost reduction. It reports what you develop. It does not report what you survive, and the distance between those two is where this deck is played.

Then take the whole thing out of here in four moves.

Keep hands that make mana in more than one colour, not hands that make nine. Deploy Dragons in waves, because you will lose one wave to somebody's sweeper and the deck rebuilds in tokens. Keep the enchantment in your hand until the turn you are actually taking, and hold something up on that turn — two thirds of the time you have the card for it.

And stop waiting for the loop. Sixty-two per cent against three point six is not a close call. The Dragons are the plan; the extra combats are a lovely thing that happens to you sometimes. Your commander, meanwhile, is going to sit in that zone all game making everything a bit easier and never once getting removed — and I still cannot prove that to you, which the Counselor is going to remind me of before we go to print.
